annotations.keyFindings: A line complication occurred in 14.6 percent of 2,114 courses through peripherally inserted central catheters, more often with vancomycin, double-lumen lines and courses longer than four weeks, mostly in the first three weeks.
annotations.limitations: Hospital records only; community-managed events missed; three centres with different line policies.

annotations.keyFindings: Midlines had fewer bloodstream infections (0.4 versus 1.4 percent) but more premature removals (11.9 versus 7.2 percent); for courses over 14 days the infection advantage shrank.
annotations.limitations: Propensity matching cannot remove confounding by the clinician's line choice; vesicants excluded from midlines.

annotations.keyFindings: Patients and carers were unsure about dressing care, delayed reporting problems for fear of seeming difficult or of readmission, and carers wanted hands-on teaching.
annotations.limitations: One service; participants chosen by the nursing team.

annotations.keyFindings: Occlusion varied from 3.1 to 11.8 percent between four nursing teams; pulsatile flushing was associated with fewer occlusions and flushing documentation was missing from 23 percent of visit notes.
annotations.limitations: Older study; incomplete documentation; team-level comparison.

annotations.keyFindings: Pooled incidence of any line complication was 9.8 per 1,000 catheter days across 38 studies; only six reported community-managed complications.
annotations.limitations: Heterogeneous definitions; mostly single-centre retrospective studies; possible reporting bias.

annotations.keyFindings: Of 140 patients asked at their first community visit, 61 could describe keeping the dressing dry and 48 knew which symptoms to report the same day; demonstration teaching did better than a leaflet.
annotations.limitations: Undated regional evaluation with no stated sampling or methods; no complication data. Method quality not assessed because no methods are reported.

annotations.keyFindings: Nurses from two agencies described late recognition between visits, unclear escalation of sluggish lines, poor out-of-hours access and inconsistent line care orders.
annotations.limitations: Two agencies; group setting may suppress dissent.

annotations.keyFindings: Line problems caused 38 percent of unplanned returns in 902 courses, concentrated in patients living alone and one agency; interviews linked the agency difference to weekend staffing and escalation.
annotations.limitations: One service; the qualitative sample was drawn from extremes, which explains variation but not typical experience.

claims.text: In 2,114 outpatient antibiotic courses through peripherally inserted central catheters, a line complication occurred in 14.6 percent of courses.
claims.passage: A line complication occurred in 14.6 percent of courses
claims.interpretation: Line problems are common enough for a local cohort of 1,870 episodes to yield a useful number of events.

claims.text: Occlusion rates ranged from 3.1 to 11.8 percent between home infusion nursing teams, and flushing documentation was missing from 23 percent of visit notes.
claims.passage: Occlusion rates ranged from 3.1 percent to 11.8 percent between teams.
claims.interpretation: Care arrangements may matter as much as line type, and agency records are needed to see them.

claims.text: In an explanatory sequential study, line problems caused 38 percent of unplanned returns, and the conversations with patients and nurses explained an agency difference by weekend staffing and escalation practice.
claims.passage: The conversations explained the agency difference by differences in weekend staffing and in how nurses escalated sluggish lines.
claims.interpretation: A quantitative strand followed by interviews sampled from its extremes has already changed priorities in a similar service.

claims.text: Hospital records miss complications managed at home: the three-centre review captured hospital events only, and only six of 38 studies in a review reported community-managed complications.
claims.passage: Only six studies reported complications managed in the community
claims.interpretation: Without the agency's visit notes the cohort will undercount complications and bias comparisons between agencies.

claims.text: Patients delayed reporting swelling or a sluggish line because they did not want to seem difficult or feared readmission.
claims.passage: Several patients delayed reporting swelling or a sluggish line because they did not want to seem difficult or feared readmission.
claims.interpretation: Delayed reporting is a mechanism the records cannot show; interviews are needed.

synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; one is an undated grey report with no stated methods (method quality not assessed). Line complications affect roughly one course in seven through peripherally inserted central catheters, with occlusion and dislodgement the most common, and line choice trades infections against premature removal. Complication rates vary several-fold between home infusion nursing teams, and hospital records miss problems handled at home. Patients delay reporting problems and nurses describe unclear escalation. One explanatory sequential study in a similar service found that interviews sampled from the extremes of a quantitative analysis explained agency differences that records alone could not. The evidence supports combining a local record-based analysis with interviews, and warns that without agency notes the quantitative strand will undercount home-managed events.
gradeRationale: Observational and qualitative evidence from single services, heterogeneous definitions and missing community data; consistent in direction on the role of care arrangements but imprecise. Certainty that any single factor drives local complications is low.
summary: Eight retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims recorded; overall certainty low; one undated record with method quality not assessed.
